learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate a critical understanding of theoretical underpinnings and debates, curriculum, legislative and policy frameworks, and pedagogical practices which make up the landscape of Indigenous education in Australia today.

Demonstrate understanding of the importance of critical and continual reflection on their professional, political and personal worldview and research-informed practices as an educator in relation to how Indigenous Australian students engage in education and learning, their peoples and cultures, and their histories and languages.
Demonstrate understanding of and reflection on Indigenous Australian education as located within broader educational frameworks, system policies, processes and contexts.
Demonstrated understandings of evidence-based teaching and learning strategies, alongside your worldview as a teacher, in relation to working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
Demonstrate a growing capacity to work effectively and respectfully within the Indigenous Australian education landscape.
Demonstrate the skills and knowledge to engage effectively and work in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities.

Work effectively and collaboratively in teams to make informed team decisions, demonstrate interpersonal, leadership and communication skills, and critically evaluate personal and peer contributions to team processes.

assessments.task_description:
Assessment task one requires you to complete a reflective journal outlining your learning and engagement with a range of materials and learning sources across this unit. Using the ‘Five Rs’ (Bain et al., 1999), you will undertake a process of process of critical self-reflection on your positionality to think critically about your learning, your responses to the learning and how you will take that forward into your practice as a teacher in the future.

You will complete three reflections in total of 400 words each (total word count: 2000).

You must have a range of examples of learning materials including:

·      Lectures

·      Tutorial activities

·      Readings

·      Online materials and activities

 

Reflections are to be written in short paragraphs and in first person. There must be evidence of engagement with:

  • theories introduced throughout the unit such as critical race theory
  • engagement of a range of course learning materials and literature including Indigenous authored sources
  • reflection on how biases and assumptions about diverse groups and worldviews affect classroom behaviour, practices, and attitudes, and how these can adversely impact specific student groups
  • application of the 5 Rs in reflecting on your learning experience
  • critical reflection on your worldview (social, cultural, political, economic) and the impact upon your reaction to engaging with Indigenous Australian peoples and learning
  • consideration of how to apply the learning from your reflection in your practice as a teacher
  • ongoing reflexivity as a mechanism for professional development and inclusive practice


Five Rs (adapted from Bain, Ballantyne, Packer & Mills, 1999)

Reporting: what was the source of the learning?

Responding: what were your feelings towards the issue? what was your initial response?

Relating: how did the learning relate to your past and current personal and or professional experiences? why was it significant in the context of learning about Indigenous education?

Reasoning: what theories are relevant in helping to understand and critically reflect on the issue? why do you think you had the initial response and what factors impacted on this?

Reconstructing: why was this a significant learning experience for you as a teacher? how will you take this learning forward into practice. How does this process support your intercultural development and reflexivity?

assessments.task_description:
Assessment task two requires you to develop a professional portfolio, which will demonstrate your acquired knowledge in addressing the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers, in particular 1.4 and 2.4. The Australian Curriculum identifies Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures as a cross-curriculum priority. The task also requires you to demonstrate your ability to embed Indigenous knowledges and perspectives in your curriculum area and discuss the theories, literature and policy that inform how and why teachers play an important role in shaping social and political discourse in Indigenous education.

To do this work effectively, teachers must engage in critical self-reflection and be proactive in identifying gaps in their knowledge and skills. As part of this portfolio, you will develop a future professional learning plan that outlines your plan to engage with a range of materials and learning to continue your professional learning and development in Indigenous education. 

Part A (500 words) (individual task)

Professional statement 

You will write a professional statement that outlines your commitment to improving Indigenous education outcomes and practices. This statement will demonstrate your understanding of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers, the Australian Curriculum cross-priority aimed at addressing improving Indigenous education outcomes and practices, and relevant Indigenous education policies. It will form part of your professional portfolio and should be written in first person. Your statement may include:

Reference to key policy and frameworks: 

• The Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (including but not limited to Standards 1.4 and 2.4)

• The Australian Curriculum cross-curriculum priority: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

• Relevant Indigenous education policies

Your professional values: 

• Describe the values that guide your teaching practice (e.g., respect, inclusion, equity, cultural responsiveness)

Commitment to reconciliation:

• Explain how your teaching will support the process of reconciliation in education

Theoretical and scholarly influences: 

• Reference theories, scholars, or literature that have shaped your understanding of Indigenous education (e.g., decolonising education, culturally sustaining pedagogy, Indigenist perspectives)

• The importance of cultural safety, including what it can look like in a classroom context

Recognition of Indigenous aspirations 

• Acknowledge the aspirations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in education, such as cultural safety, academic success, and self-determination and strategies used to implement and achieve this

Acknowledgement of diversity

• Demonstrate an understanding of the diversity within and across First Nations peoples, including differences in culture, language, perspectives, and the historical and ongoing impacts of colonisation

• Demonstrate strategies on how you will work in collaboration with local Indigenous community members to include place based Indigenous knowledges (CC 4.1.3 – practised)


Part B (2000 words) (group task)

Lesson plans and rationale (this task connects with Assessment task 3)

In a group of three or four, develop two lesson plans that clearly demonstrate your ability to embed Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives into curriculum. You may use a lesson plan template used in your curriculum area, but all lesson plans must include:


• Learning objectives, year level, and key learning area

• Time frame

• Pedagogical adjustments

• Indigenous material and resources used (with evidence of rigorous selection of the type of resources used)

• Practical strategies that reflect and promote cultural safety in classroom environments

• Mechanisms for evaluation of the lesson


Rationale

The rationale is to be written in third person. It will address the reasons why it is important for teachers to be capable and confident in addressing issues in Indigenous education, including engaging effectively and collaboratively with Indigenous students, families and communities, embedding Indigenous perspectives and how to teach Indigenous students. Using scholarly sources, address the following:

• Why it is important for teachers to recognise and respond to the diversity within and across First Nations peoples, including differences in culture, language, historical experience, and perspectives

• Research evidence on the positive impacts of engaging with First Nations families and communities to support learning outcomes

• Why it is important for teachers to engage and work in partnership with Indigenous peoples and communities to include First Nations knowledges. 

• How Indigenous education policy, theories, and literature can shape teaching practice

• How embedding Indigenous knowledges and perspectives addresses issues in Indigenous education and broader social issues

• Why cultural safety is required and strategies used to implement this in the classroom.


Part C (500 words) (individual task)

Indigenous Education professional development 

This section can be written in first person. It allows you to self-assess gaps that might still exist in your understanding of Australian histories, your culture and standpoint, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and histories and Indigenous education frameworks and approaches. You may identify materials from a range of sources including:

• Indigenous community events and organisations 

• Professional development sessions

• Books

• Web based resources

• Documentaries 

A suggested template for your plan is available on Blackboard Ultra.

assessments.task_description:
Building on your planned activity for Task 2, in your group, select key elements of your lesson plan and teach a condensed version of the lesson. This task gives you an opportunity to trial and refine your lesson plan by translating your ideas into practice within a microteaching context. It provides a chance to receive feedback on your planned strategies for embedding Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives. The task also includes a structured peer interaction component, where you respond to questions and engage in professional discussion to justify and strengthen your teaching decisions.


Part A: Microteaching episode (approx. 10 minutes)

In your group, your teaching must demonstrate:

·        Clear learning objectives appropriate to the chosen year level and learning area

·        Meaningful and accurate inclusion of Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives

·        Use of carefully selected Indigenous resources/materials

·        Culturally safe teaching practices, including respectful language and representation

·        Appropriate pedagogical strategies (e.g., scaffolding, questioning, modelling)

·        Pedagogical adjustments to support diverse learners

·        Active student engagement strategies


Part B: Professional Explanation and Interaction (approx. 5 minutes)

Following your microteaching, your group will participate in a short whole-class interaction (Q&A and discussion). Your group will be expected to:

·        Briefly explain the intent and context of the lesson

·        Justify your selection of Indigenous perspectives and resources

·        Explain how your teaching promotes cultural safety and respect

·        Describe how the lesson could be adapted for different learners

·        Respond thoughtfully and professionally to peer and tutor questions

How this is marked:

This task is a Pass/Fail hurdle for the course. Your group will receive a single mark for this task and you will be provided with a copy of the Pass/Fail rubric in advance. This assessment will be recorded in line with academic policy.
